nama_domain: Gaming & Esports Industry (mobile-first gaming, esports professionalization, and the state's protective regulation of minors in games)
tahun_mulai_china: Layered timeline. (1) Industry base: online gaming became a mass phenomenon in China from 2001-2005 via PC internet cafes (wangba) and Shanda/NetEase MMOs; esports was recognized by the General Administration of Sport as China's 99th official sport in 2003. (2) Mobile-first inflection: 2013-2016, driven by 4G rollout, WeChat/QQ distribution and Tencent's Honor of Kings (launched November 2015, mass breakout 2016). (3) Esports institutionalization: 2016 is the pivotal year — the King Pro League (KPL) launched, LPL franchised, and in September 2016 the Ministry of Education added 'Esports and Management' (电子竞技运动与管理) to the vocational higher-education catalogue for implementation from 2017. (4) The regulatory/protective phase — the part Indonesia is lagging on — began in 2018 (nine-month approval freeze, August 2018 anti-myopia notice) and hardened in November 2019 (NPPA anti-addiction notice: 90 min/weekday, 3h/holiday, curfew 22:00-08:00, age-tiered spending caps) and definitively on 30 August 2021 (one hour on Fri/Sat/Sun/public holidays only, 20:00-21:00).
pemain_kunci_china: Publishers/developers: Tencent (Honor of Kings, Peacekeeper Elite, League of Legends via Riot, PUBG Mobile via Krafton partnership), NetEase (Identity V, Naraka, Eggy Party), miHoYo/HoYoverse (Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, Zenless Zone Zero), ByteDance (Nuverse + Moonton/Mobile Legends: Bang Bang, acquired 2021, agreed sold to Saudi Savvy Games Group for >USD 6bn on 20 March 2026), Perfect World, 37 Interactive Entertainment, Lilith Games, XD Inc., Game Science (Black Myth: Wukong, 2024), Century Huatong/Dianhun, Yoozoo, FunPlus, IGG. Distribution/streaming: WeChat Mini Games, Douyin mini-games, Huya, DouYu, Bilibili, TapTap. Esports: LPL, KPL, EDG (2021 LoL Worlds champion), JD Gaming, Bilibili Gaming, Weibo Gaming, Team WE; host cities Shanghai (declared 'global esports capital', 2017), Hangzhou (Asian Games 2022/2023 medal esports), Chengdu, Xi'an. Regulators/industry bodies: National Press and Publication Administration (NPPA — issues banhao/version numbers), Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS), CADPA Game Publishing Committee (GPC) and Gamma Data (伽马数据) as the official statistical authority.
apa_yang_terjadi_di_china:
China built the world's largest games market and then deliberately capped its social externalities — a full cycle of boom, backlash, and state-engineered restraint that Indonesia has not yet passed through.

MECHANISM OF THE BOOM (2013-2020): Cheap 4G, a smartphone-only user base skipping consoles, and super-app distribution (WeChat/QQ) made mobile the default. Tencent's Honor of Kings turned a 5v5 MOBA into a mass social ritual, and the free-to-play + gacha/battle-pass monetization model replaced upfront purchase. Esports was deliberately built as a legitimizing layer on top of gaming: franchised leagues (LPL, KPL), city-based teams with local government subsidies (Shanghai, Hangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an each issued esports industry policies and built dedicated arenas), and streaming platforms (Huya/DouYu/Bilibili) that converted viewership into the industry's largest revenue line.

MECHANISM OF THE BACKLASH (2018-2021): The state's concern was not economic but demographic and social — youth myopia, academic performance, family conflict, and 'game addiction'. Instruments used, in escalating order: (a) the banhao/version-number licensing chokepoint — every commercially monetized game requires an approval number, and approvals were frozen for nine months in 2018 and again from July 2021 to April 2022, which is the single most powerful lever the state holds; (b) mandatory real-name registration against the national ID database, later reinforced by Tencent's facial-recognition 'Midnight Patrol' (2021) that challenges night-time players whose behaviour looks underage; (c) hard playtime windows for under-18s (Nov 2019: 90 min weekdays / 3h holidays, 22:00-08:00 curfew; 30 Aug 2021: one hour on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays only, 20:00-21:00 — roughly 3 hours per week, down from 13.5); (d) age-tiered in-game spending caps for minors; (e) content controls (no blood, no explicit gambling mechanics, historical-accuracy requirements); (f) mandatory loot-box/gacha probability disclosure since the Ministry of Culture's interim measures effective 1 May 2017 — a world-first that predates Western loot-box debates by years; (g) rhetorical shock therapy — a Xinhua-affiliated Economic Information Daily article on 3 August 2021 branded games 'spiritual opium' (精神鸦片) and named Honor of Kings, wiping roughly USD 60bn off Tencent's market value in a day; (h) legal codification — the revised Law on the Protection of Minors (effective 1 June 2021) added an Internet Protection chapter, and the State Council's Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Cyberspace took effect 1 January 2024.

CONSOLIDATION AND RECOVERY (2022-2026): Approvals resumed in April 2022 and are now issued in predictable monthly batches (including regular batches of imported titles), which the industry reads as normalization rather than liberalization. A December 2023 NPPA draft ('Measures for the Administration of Online Games') proposing monthly spending caps (~RMB 400), a ban on daily-login and consecutive-recharge rewards, and a ban on item auctions erased roughly USD 80bn from Tencent and NetEase in one session; the draft was pulled from the NPPA website in January 2024 and never enacted — an important signal that even China's regulator now trades off child protection against a strategically valuable export industry. The market resumed growth: domestic sales revenue reached RMB 350.79bn in 2025 (+7.68% y/y) with 683m users, and self-developed Chinese games earned USD 20.45bn overseas in 2025. Growth has shifted decisively toward (i) mini-games inside WeChat/Douyin (RMB 53.5bn, +34.4% in 2025, over half of all incremental market growth), (ii) premium single-player console/PC titles after Black Myth: Wukong (2024), and (iii) overseas expansion — which is precisely the channel through which the trend reaches Indonesia.

ESPORTS AS A MATURE, PLATEAUED SECTOR: China's esports industry earned RMB 29.33bn in 2025 (+6.4%), but its audience of 495.3m has been essentially flat since 2021 (489.2m), and 80.8% of industry income comes from livestreaming rather than tickets, sponsorship or media rights. Mobile titles are 58.6% of esports revenue. Esports in China has completed the arc from subculture to state-sanctioned sport (Asian Games medal event, Hangzhou 2023) to a mature, consolidating industry with a well-documented oversupply of aspiring professionals relative to paid roles.
data_skala_china:
MARKET: Domestic games market actual sales revenue RMB 350.789bn in 2025 (+7.68% y/y), per the 2025 China Game Industry Report (CADPA Game Publishing Committee + Gamma Data, released at the annual conference in Shanghai, 17-19 December 2025). Users: 683m (+1.35% y/y) — user growth is now effectively saturated at roughly 1-1.5% per year. Mini-games: RMB 53.535bn in 2025 (+34.39%), of which in-app purchase RMB 36.464bn (68.1%) and advertising RMB 17.071bn (31.9%); WeChat Mini Games alone reported ~571m MAU and 70 titles above 1m DAU in 2025; the mini-game segment is forecast to pass RMB 70bn in 2026. EXPORT: overseas sales revenue of self-developed Chinese games exceeded USD 20.45bn in 2025; self-developed mobile games overseas reached ~USD 18.47bn (+13.16%); the US takes ~32% of Chinese mobile game export revenue, Japan ~16%, South Korea ~9% [uncertain on the Southeast Asia share, which is not consistently broken out].

ESPORTS: industry income RMB 29.331bn in 2025 (+6.4% y/y, ~USD 4.02bn); audience 495.3m (+1.06%), up from 489.2m in 2021 — only ~6m added in four years; livestreaming = 80.81% of esports industry income; by genre, shooters 28.3%, MOBA 14.1%, sports 14.1%; by platform, mobile 58.6%, PC client 25.3%.

REGULATORY IMPACT: 2018 approval freeze lasted ~9 months and cut close to USD 200bn from Tencent's market capitalization at its trough. The July 2021-April 2022 freeze coincided with the closure of roughly 14,000 gaming studios/gaming-related firms (some reports cite up to 140,000 when advertising, publishing and merchandising firms are included) — the 14,000 vs 140,000 divergence reflects different definitions of 'gaming-related firm'. The 3 August 2021 'spiritual opium' article cost Tencent roughly USD 60bn in market value in one day. The December 2023 draft spending-cap rules erased roughly USD 80bn from Tencent and NetEase before being withdrawn.

MINOR PROTECTION OUTCOMES: after the September 2021 rules, CADPA/Gamma reported (November 2022) that more than 75% of minor gamers play less than three hours per week and declared the addiction problem 'basically resolved'. Minors' contribution to Tencent's domestic game gross receipts fell to a low single-digit fraction of a percent [uncertain — Tencent has reported figures around 0.4-1.0% in various quarters]. Pre-restriction baseline: minors were allowed up to 13.5 hours/week under the 2019 rules; the 2021 rules cut this to 3 hours/week — a 78% reduction by regulation alone.
fase_tren_di_china: REGULATED + MATURE, with a re-growth phase inside the regulatory cage. The consumption boom peaked around 2020-2021; the backlash phase ran 2018-2022 and culminated in the Aug 2021 minor restrictions and the licence freeze; since April 2022 the sector has been in a 'managed normalization' phase — record revenue (RMB 350.8bn in 2025) but saturated users (+1.35%), consolidated ownership, and growth displaced into mini-games, premium PC/console titles, and exports. Esports specifically is MATURE/PLATEAUED (audience flat since 2021, revenue growing single digits, heavy dependence on livestreaming). Minor-protection policy is in a STABLE ENFORCED phase — no evidence of relaxation as of mid-2026 — while monetization policy is in a DEREGULATORY PAUSE after the December 2023 draft was withdrawn.
puncak_tren_china: Multiple peaks depending on the dimension. (a) User-growth peak: 2020-2021 (COVID lockdowns pushed users past 660m; growth then collapsed to ~1%/year). (b) Regulatory-intensity peak: August-September 2021 — the 'spiritual opium' article (3 Aug 2021), the NPPA one-hour rule (30 Aug 2021), and the simultaneous licence freeze; geographically centred on Beijing (NPPA/CAC) and Shenzhen (Tencent). (c) Esports peak: 2021-2022 — EDG's LoL Worlds title (November 2021) triggered nationwide campus celebrations and is the cultural high-water mark; audience has been flat since. Host-city peak: Shanghai (LPL/KPL hub, 'global esports capital' policy from 2017) and Hangzhou (Asian Games 2023, where esports became a full medal event). (d) Revenue peak: not yet reached — 2025 was a record year (RMB 350.8bn), so the industry peak is ahead, but per-user and per-title economics peaked earlier. (e) Esports-education peak: 2017-2019, when ~30-50 vocational colleges opened esports programmes; enrolment enthusiasm has since cooled as graduate placement disappointed.
status_di_indonesia: SPLIT STATUS — this is the key analytical point. On CONSUMPTION, Indonesia is already massively in (near-zero lag; arguably simultaneous with China, since Mobile Legends launched in Indonesia in 2016, the same year Honor of Kings broke out in China). On ESPORTS, Indonesia is fully mainstream and state-recognized (esports is an official olahraga prestasi under Kemenpora/KONI, with PBESI as the national federation). On DOMESTIC PRODUCTION, Indonesia is a laggard/dependent market — local developers capture under 1-5% of domestic spending. On PROTECTIVE REGULATION OF MINORS — the specific subject of this research item — Indonesia is BARU MULAI (just beginning): PP 17/2025 ('PP Tunas') was signed 28 March 2025 and the Indonesia Game Rating System was relaunched 11 October 2025 with mandatory effect from 2026, roughly six years after China's equivalent 2019 measures and with materially weaker instruments (age tiers and parental consent, but no playtime curfew, no state-run real-name gaming ID, no spending caps).
contoh_konkret_indonesia: CONSUMPTION/PLATFORMS: Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (Moonton; Indonesia is MLBB's largest market worldwide, 35m+ MAU, ~40.5% of active Indonesian mobile players), Garena Free Fire (Sea Group), PUBG Mobile, Honor of Kings (Level Infinite/Tencent), Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail (HoYoverse), Roblox, EA FC Mobile. ESPORTS: PBESI (Pengurus Besar Esports Indonesia, the Kemenpora-recognized federation), MPL Indonesia (Season 16 ran 22 Aug-2 Nov 2025 with nine franchised teams), Liga Esports Nasional, teams RRQ, EVOS, ONIC, Bigetron, Alter Ego, Aura, Dewa United, Kagendra (sent to Honor of Kings World Cup 2025 with Menpora send-off); EVOS Divine won Free Fire at the Esports World Cup 2025 (USD 300,000). PAYMENTS/INFRASTRUCTURE: UniPin (Indonesian top-up gateway), Codashop, warnet/gaming-cafe chains, Telkomsel/Indosat gaming data packages. LOCAL STUDIOS: Agate International (Bandung), Toge Productions (Coffee Talk, A Space for the Unbound), Digital Happiness (DreadOut), Mojiken Studio, Ozysoft, Anantarupa (Lokapala — the first Indonesian MOBA, built on local mythology). POLICY: Perpres 19/2024 on Acceleration of National Game Industry Development (signed 12 February 2024, eight pillars: research, education, funding, infrastructure, marketing, incentives, IP facilitation, protection of creative output); Permenkominfo 2/2024 on game classification (replacing Permenkominfo 11/2016 which created IGRS); PP 17/2025 'PP Tunas' on child protection in digital space (signed 28 March 2025, effective 1 April 2025, phased platform obligations from 28 March 2026); IGRS enforcement drive from 11 October 2025, mandatory 2026, with Komdigi publicly investigating rating mismatches on Steam.
data_skala_indonesia:
MARKET SIZE (sources conflict — see catatan_kontradiksi_data): commonly cited figures are USD 4.28bn for 2025 with ~8% CAGR to 2029 (industry/Xsolla-type estimates), versus a Kemenperin/industry-study figure of roughly USD 2.0-2.5bn (about Rp 41.3 trillion) for the domestic market, versus a narrower Statista 2023 figure of USD 1.117bn. Indonesia is the largest games market in Southeast Asia, contributing roughly 45.8% of the regional market, and ranks around 16th globally by revenue but in the global top ten by player count.

PLAYERS: commonly cited at 155m (on a 274m population base) rising toward ~190-192m by 2025 [uncertain — 'gamer' definitions include casual mobile players]. Platform split: ~83% of Indonesian gamers play on smartphones, ~34% on PC, ~21% on console — one of the most mobile-skewed major markets in the world.

LOCAL PRODUCTION: Kemenperin data (cited 2021) put local developers at 0.4% of domestic game spending; a 2025-2026 study put local developers at ~5% of a ~USD 2bn market with 95% captured by foreign publishers; another study (October 2025) framed it as 99.5% foreign vs 0.5% local. Whichever number is used, Indonesia is a consumption colony rather than a production hub. Stated barriers: limited capital, thin developer pool, and technical skill gaps in programming and game design.

ESPORTS: market estimates diverge wildly (from USD ~1.8bn in 2025 with a 24% CAGR down to figures in the tens of millions), which indicates definitional chaos [uncertain]. Verifiable hard numbers: MLBB generated USD 4.701m in prize money across Indonesian-relevant circuits; Indonesia topped the SEA Esports Nations Cup 2026 medal table.

DIGITAL PRECONDITIONS: internet penetration 80.66% in 2025 (APJII), 229.4m users on ~284m population, up from 79.50% in 2024; 83.39% of internet users access via smartphone (95% of the population's access is mobile-first); urban penetration 83.56% vs rural 76.96%; Gen Z is 25.54% of users, Millennials 25.17%, Gen Alpha 23.19% — meaning roughly a quarter of Indonesia's online population is under 13.

HARM DATA (the reason regulation is now moving): Komdigi reported in 2026 that nearly 200,000 Indonesian children have been exposed to online gambling. Kemenkes/hospital data show a 28% increase in psychiatric visits by children and adolescents aged 7-18 for gadget addiction in Oct-Nov 2025 versus the same period in 2024. RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan (Jakarta) recorded 1,856 such visits, up from 1,450, of which 62% were online-game addiction and 31% pornography exposure. RSJ Menur (Surabaya) has treated around 3,000 child and adolescent patients for gadget/online-game addiction and has exceeded inpatient capacity for addiction cases. Roughly 54 psychiatric hospitals nationwide now handle internet, game and online-gambling addiction.
estimasi_lag_tahun:
Dimension-dependent — a single number is misleading:
(1) CONSUMPTION / mobile-gaming penetration: 0-2 years lag, effectively SIMULTANEOUS. MLBB launched in Indonesia in 2016, the same year Honor of Kings broke out in China; Indonesian players receive Chinese-developed content in the same global release windows.
(2) ESPORTS PROFESSIONALIZATION: ~2-4 years. China institutionalized esports in 2016 (KPL, MOE major); Indonesia's PBESI/Kemenpora recognition and MPL franchising landed 2019-2020; esports reached the Asian Games as a demonstration event in 2018 (Jakarta) — Indonesia was actually a co-author of that milestone.
(3) PROTECTIVE REGULATION OF MINORS: 5-7 years, and structurally weaker. China: real-name + curfew rules Nov 2019, hard one-hour rule Aug 2021, Cyberspace Minor Protection Regulations Jan 2024. Indonesia: PP 17/2025 (March 2025), IGRS mandatory enforcement 2026. That is roughly six years behind China's 2019 baseline — and Indonesia's version contains no playtime curfew, no spending cap, and no state-operated real-name gaming database, so on instrument strength the effective lag is closer to 8-10 years, or arguably permanent if Indonesia never adopts curfews.
(4) DOMESTIC PRODUCTION CAPABILITY: 12-18 years. China's domestic developers took roughly 85%+ of domestic spending by the mid-2010s and now export USD 20bn+; Indonesian studios hold 0.5-5% of their own market. This is the widest and most consequential gap.
(5) LOOT-BOX/GACHA PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE: China mandated this from 1 May 2017; Indonesia has no equivalent binding mandate as of mid-2026 — a 9+ year lag with no announced closure date.
bukti_historical_lag:
(a) SOCIAL MEDIA / SHORT VIDEO PRECEDENT: China restricted minors on Douyin via 'teen mode' and a 40-minute youth mode (2019-2021); Indonesia only produced binding child-protection rules for high-risk digital platforms with PP 17/2025 (effective platform obligations from March 2026) — a comparable ~6 year regulatory lag, and Indonesia explicitly cited overseas precedent (Australia's under-16 social media ban, EU DSA, China's minor mode) rather than originating the design.
(b) ONLINE GAMBLING: China effectively eliminated consumer-facing online gambling early through payment-rail and ISP blocking; Indonesia's judi online crisis exploded 2023-2025 with hundreds of trillions of rupiah in transactions and required an emergency task force in 2024 — showing Indonesian regulation is reactive (post-harm) rather than preemptive.
(c) FINTECH/P2P LENDING: China's P2P sector peaked 2015-2017 and was fully wound down by 2020 after mass defaults; Indonesia's pinjol boom peaked 2021-2024 and OJK tightening followed the harm — a ~4-6 year lag with the same reactive pattern.
(d) RIDE-HAILING/GIG: Didi's driver-welfare rules (2021) preceded Indonesia's ojol THR/welfare debates (2024-2025) by ~3-4 years.
(e) WITHIN GAMING ITSELF: China's Ministry of Culture mandated gacha probability disclosure effective 1 May 2017; Indonesia's IGRS (introduced 2016 under Permenkominfo 11/2016) sat largely unenforced for nearly a decade until the October 2025 relaunch — showing that Indonesia can adopt the paper instrument early but lags China by many years on enforcement capacity, which is the real binding variable.
(f) The consistent historical pattern: Indonesia imports the consumption trend at near-zero lag but imports the protective regulation at a 5-7 year lag, because the consumption trend arrives through commercial channels (app stores, ads) that require no state action, while regulation requires state capacity that Indonesia builds only after visible harm.
tipe_lag: MIXED / ASYMMETRIC. Consumption: SIMULTANEOUS (Indonesia is a first-wave market for Chinese mobile games, not a follower). Esports: SIMULTANEOUS-to-slightly-LAGGARD, with a genuine REVERSE element — Indonesia hosted esports as an Asian Games demonstration sport in 2018 before China's Hangzhou 2023 medal event, and Indonesia is MLBB's global number-one market, so Indonesian scene dynamics sometimes lead rather than follow. Protective regulation: clear LAGGARD (5-7 years). Domestic production capability: severe LAGGARD (12-18 years) with no leapfrog visible. The overall label most useful for policy is 'consumption-simultaneous, regulation-laggard, production-laggard' — Indonesia absorbs the full social cost of a mature Chinese industry while capturing almost none of its industrial value.
probabilitas_transfer: Tinggi (High) — but with an important qualification: the commercial side has ALREADY transferred completely; what is still in transit is the REGULATORY side, and that is arriving in a diluted, non-Chinese form.
alasan_probabilitas:
COMMERCIAL SIDE — already 100% transferred, probability moot. Chinese-developed or Chinese-owned titles dominate Indonesian mobile gaming (MLBB via Moonton, PUBG Mobile and Honor of Kings via Tencent/Level Infinite, Genshin/Star Rail via HoYoverse, plus a long tail of Chinese-published hyper-casual and 4X titles). Chinese exports of self-developed games hit USD 20.45bn in 2025 and Southeast Asia is a priority region because of demographic fit, mobile-only device profiles, and cultural proximity in art style. Indonesia's 229m internet users and 80%+ mobile-first access make it the single biggest Southeast Asian prize.

REGULATORY SIDE — high probability of arrival but low probability of arriving in China's form. Drivers pushing it: (i) documented and rising harm (28% y/y increase in child psychiatric visits for gadget addiction; ~200,000 children exposed to online gambling); (ii) political salience of judi online, which has made 'games = gateway to gambling' a live parliamentary and DPD issue; (iii) international precedent cascade (Australia's under-16 social media ban, EU DSA, UK Online Safety Act) giving Indonesian regulators cover; (iv) an existing legal vehicle already in place (PP 17/2025 + Permenkominfo 2/2024 + IGRS) that only requires tightening rather than new primary legislation; (v) Komdigi's demonstrated willingness to block platforms, which gives it credible enforcement leverage over app stores.

Counterweights that make full Chinese-style copying unlikely: Indonesia has no equivalent of the banhao licensing chokepoint (games reach Indonesians through Google Play, the App Store and Steam, not a national approval queue); Indonesia has no unified, enforced real-name identity layer binding game accounts to NIK; and Indonesia's political economy treats gaming and esports as a growth sector to be promoted (Perpres 19/2024) rather than a social ill to be suppressed, so the state's own incentives are contradictory in a way China's were not in 2021.

MINI-GAMES / IN-APP GAME PLATFORMS — high probability, medium timeline. China's mini-game explosion (RMB 53.5bn, +34.4% in 2025) is the clearest next-wave trend with a real lag, and its natural Indonesian carriers already exist: TikTok's in-app games, WhatsApp/Telegram-adjacent casual play, and super-app surfaces (GoPay/Gojek, Grab, Shopee). Expect it in Indonesia in force 2027-2029.
vektor_transmisi:
(a) DIRECT ENTRY BY CHINESE PLAYERS — dominant vector, already complete. Tencent (Level Infinite regional publishing, plus a longstanding stake in Sea Group which publishes Garena Free Fire, Indonesia's other top mobile title), HoYoverse (Singapore-based regional HQ serving Indonesia), Moonton (Shanghai-founded, ByteDance-owned 2021-2026, agreed sale to Savvy Games Group announced 20 March 2026 — note this means MLBB's future ownership is Saudi, not Chinese, a genuine change in the transmission map), NetEase, 37 Interactive, Lilith, FunPlus, and dozens of smaller Chinese publishers running Indonesian localization, Indonesian-language community management, and Ramadan/Independence-Day themed events. Chinese publishers also run Jakarta-based marketing and community offices and hire Indonesian country managers.

(b) LOCAL COPYCAT / DERIVATIVE PRODUCTION — weak but real. Indonesian studios (Anantarupa's Lokapala, an MOBA built on Nusantara mythology) explicitly copy Chinese-validated genre templates with local IP skins. The bigger copycat wave is on the business-model side: Indonesian top-up merchants, gacha-style promo mechanics in non-game apps, and battle-pass structures in Indonesian e-commerce and fintech gamification. Expect Indonesian mini-game studios cloning Chinese WeChat mini-game hits for TikTok/super-app surfaces from 2027.

(c) ALGORITHMIC CONTENT DIFFUSION — very high intensity. TikTok (Indonesia is TikTok's largest or second-largest market), YouTube Shorts, and Chinese-origin livestreaming formats push gacha-pull reaction videos, meta guides, and top-up promos into Indonesian feeds continuously. Indonesian gaming creators mirror Douyin/Bilibili content formats. This vector transmits the monetization CULTURE (whale spending norms, gacha FOMO, streak mechanics) faster than any company entry.

(d) CHINESE VENTURE CAPITAL — moderate. Tencent's stake in Sea Group and historic investments in Gojek/GoTo, Chinese participation in Indonesian esports team and gaming-media funding rounds, and Chinese-backed payment/top-up rails. Note the vector is partially diverted: Gulf capital (Savvy Games Group, Qiddiya) is now competing with Chinese capital for Southeast Asian gaming assets, as the Moonton sale shows.

(e) DIASPORA / ALUMNI / TALENT — moderate and growing. Indonesian nationals working at Chinese publishers' Singapore and Shanghai offices, Indonesian esports players and coaches in Chinese-run leagues, and Indonesian art/animation outsourcing studios servicing Chinese clients (the Vietnam-style outsourcing path). Chinese esports operators also import tournament-production know-how directly.

(f) POLICY DIFFUSION — the vector specific to the regulatory half of this trend. Indonesian regulators study China, Australia, the EU and South Korea (which repealed its own shutdown law in 2021 — a cautionary precedent Indonesia is also aware of). Komdigi's PP Tunas design borrows the age-tier + parental-consent architecture from the EU/UK rather than China's curfew architecture, which is why the transferred product looks different from the Chinese original.
prasyarat_struktural:
THRESHOLDS FOR THE CONSUMPTION TREND (already cleared by Indonesia):
- Smartphone penetration above ~60% of population: China crossed this around 2015-2016; Indonesia crossed it around 2019-2021 and is at ~80.66% internet penetration with 229.4m users (APJII 2025), 83-95% mobile-first access. CLEARED.
- Affordable mobile data (<2% of monthly income for a usable bundle): China cleared this with the 2015-2017 'speed up, cut fees' campaign; Indonesia has among the cheapest mobile data in Asia. CLEARED — and this is precisely why a 17-year-old in Bangka Belitung could consume 30GB/month on Free Fire alone.
- Digital micropayment rails: China had WeChat Pay/Alipay by 2014-2015; Indonesia now has QRIS, GoPay, OVO, DANA plus pulsa-based top-up and UniPin/Codashop vouchers. CLEARED, arguably more accessible than China's because pulsa top-up requires no bank account or ID.
- Youth demographic bulge: China's gaming boom rode a large 15-35 cohort; Indonesia's median age is ~30 with Gen Z + Gen Alpha at ~49% of internet users. CLEARED, more favourable than China today.
- GDP per capita: this is where the divergence matters. China's per-capita GDP was roughly USD 8,000-12,600 across its 2016-2021 gaming peak; Indonesia is around USD 5,000 in 2025 [uncertain — figure not verified in this research]. Indonesia is therefore at roughly China's 2013-2015 income level while consuming China's 2025 content. Consequence: Indonesian ARPU is a fraction of China's, the market is ad-monetized and low-spend rather than whale-driven, and mini-games/hyper-casual (ad-funded) fit Indonesia better than premium gacha.
- Urbanization: China was ~57% urban in 2016; Indonesia is ~58-59% now. CLEARED.

THRESHOLDS FOR THE REGULATORY TREND (partially cleared — this is the binding constraint):
- Visible, quantified harm: CLEARED as of 2025-2026 (hospital admission statistics, judi online exposure figures).
- A functioning national digital identity layer that can be bound to game accounts: NOT CLEARED. China's real-name system rests on a universal, verified, queryable ID database plus platform-side facial recognition. Indonesia has NIK/Dukcapil and is building INA Digital/IKD, but there is no mandated, low-friction game-account-to-NIK binding, and enforcement against foreign app stores is untested.
- Regulatory chokepoint over distribution: NOT CLEARED. Without a banhao equivalent, Indonesia can only regulate at the app-store, payment-rail or ISP-blocking layer, all of which are blunter and easier to route around (VPN, third-party APK, foreign card top-up).
- Enforcement capacity and inspection staffing: WEAK. Komdigi's IGRS enforcement against Steam ratings in late 2025 was the first real test.
- Political consensus that gaming is a harm rather than an industry: NOT PRESENT. Perpres 19/2024 makes the government a promoter of the industry, creating an internal contradiction China did not have.

THRESHOLDS FOR DOMESTIC PRODUCTION (not cleared, and the reason lag persists):
- A pipeline of 10,000+ trained game engineers/technical artists: China had this by ~2010 via a large CS graduate base and outsourcing apprenticeship; Indonesia's game-related graduate output is in the low thousands per year at best [uncertain].
- Patient domestic capital willing to fund 3-5 year game development cycles: absent; Indonesian studios rely on personal savings, publisher advances or foreign capital.
- A domestic publisher with global distribution: absent.
- Government procurement/subsidy at scale (Chinese city esports subsidies ran into hundreds of millions of RMB per city): Perpres 19/2024 provides the framework but implementing regulations and budget lines are thin.
indikator_pemantauan:
REGULATORY TIGHTENING (watch these to know when Chinese-style restriction is actually arriving):
1. Publication of implementing regulations (Permen/Kepmen Komdigi) under PP 17/2025 that specify verification methods — especially any requirement to bind game accounts to NIK or to use device-level age signals from Google Play/App Store.
2. Any draft mentioning 'batas waktu bermain' (playtime limits), 'jam malam digital' (digital curfew), or 'batas pembelian dalam gim' (in-game spending caps) — the presence of these three phrases in a Komdigi/DPR draft is the single clearest signal of Chinese-style transfer.
3. Mandatory gacha probability disclosure requirements appearing in IGRS technical standards.
4. Komdigi enforcement actions: number of games delisted, app-store takedown requests, and IGRS non-compliance sanctions issued after the 2026 mandatory date. The Steam rating investigation (late 2025) is the baseline case.
5. DPR/DPD Panja or RUU on child digital protection or on gaming/judi online convergence.
6. Whether Indonesian courts or OJK begin treating gacha/loot boxes as gambling under KUHP/judi online enforcement — a single such ruling would move faster than any Komdigi regulation.

INDUSTRY/COMMERCIAL:
7. Chinese publisher local entity registrations (PT PMA) and Jakarta office openings; Level Infinite / HoYoverse / NetEase Indonesian job postings for country manager, community manager, localization lead.
8. Trademark filings at DJKI for Chinese game titles and esports league brands.
9. Appearance of mini-game surfaces inside Indonesian super-apps (TikTok Indonesia in-app games, GoPay/Shopee/Grab game tabs) — the leading indicator for the mini-game wave.
10. Top-up transaction volumes at UniPin/Codashop and telco gaming bundle attach rates.
11. Esports franchise slot prices in MPL/Liga Esports Nasional and sponsorship mix shifting from crypto/gambling-adjacent to mainstream FMCG/banking brands (a maturity indicator).

EDUCATION/LABOUR:
12. New prodi approvals at Kemendikti Saintek for game technology, game design, and esports management; SMK jurusan gim enrolment numbers.
13. Job-posting volume on LinkedIn/Glints for 'Unity developer', 'Unreal', 'technical artist', 'LiveOps', 'game economy designer' based in Indonesia.
14. Growth of art/animation outsourcing contracts from Chinese and Japanese publishers to Indonesian studios (the Vietnam path).

HARM/SOCIAL:
15. Kemenkes/RSJ quarterly data on child and adolescent admissions for gaming and gambling addiction — currently the fastest-moving indicator (+28% y/y).
16. Google Trends volume in Indonesia for 'cara berhenti main game', 'kecanduan game anak', 'top up gratis', 'akun gacor'.
17. Number of psychiatric hospitals establishing dedicated behavioural-addiction units (currently ~54 handling addiction cases generally).
hambatan_transfer:
FOR THE REGULATORY HALF (why Chinese-style rules are slow to arrive):
- No licensing chokepoint. Without a banhao equivalent, Indonesia cannot condition market access on compliance; it can only ask global app stores to cooperate, and app stores answer to their own global policies first.
- No enforceable real-name layer. Chinese enforcement rests on a queryable national ID plus facial recognition; Indonesia's IKD/INA Digital is not integrated with game accounts, and pulsa/voucher top-ups are deliberately ID-free.
- Circumvention is trivial and culturally normalized. VPNs, third-party APK stores, foreign-region accounts, and account-sharing are already common; even in China, minors routinely borrow adult IDs, and Indonesia has none of China's compensating surveillance.
- Institutional contradiction. Perpres 19/2024 makes the state an active promoter of the game industry and esports (Kemenpora, Kemenparekraf/Kemenekraf, Kemenperin), while Komdigi and Kemenkes push restriction. There is no single ministry with both mandate and capacity.
- Enforcement staffing and technical capacity at Komdigi is thin relative to hundreds of thousands of distributed titles.
- Political economy of parents. In China the 2021 crackdown had broad parental support amid gaokao pressure; in Indonesia, smartphones are often the cheapest childcare available to working-class families, and blanket restriction faces quieter but real resistance.
- Cultural framing. Gaming in Indonesia is celebrated as a national-pride vehicle (SEA Games medals, MPL, MLBB world championships) rather than framed as 'spiritual opium'; there is no dominant negative narrative to mobilize.
- Regional cautionary precedent. South Korea repealed its Cinderella Law shutdown in 2021 after a decade, which Indonesian policymakers and industry lobbyists cite against curfews.

FOR THE PRODUCTION HALF (why local industry stays small):
- Capital scarcity and no patient funding for 3-5 year dev cycles.
- Talent thinness: shortage of senior engine programmers, technical artists, and game economy designers; brain drain to Singapore.
- No domestic publisher with global distribution or UA (user acquisition) budgets — Chinese publishers spend more on Indonesian user acquisition than Indonesian studios' entire budgets.
- Weak IP monetization ecosystem (merchandise, licensing) and piracy norms.
- Payment friction for premium products; the market is conditioned to free-to-play.
faktor_pembatal_transfer:
Conditions that will prevent China's version of this trend from ever landing in Indonesia in the same form:

1. ABSENCE OF A SOVEREIGN DISTRIBUTION LAYER. China's entire regulatory architecture is downstream of one fact: the Great Firewall plus the banhao system means the Chinese state controls which games exist domestically. Indonesia's games reach users through Google Play, the App Store and Steam — infrastructures Indonesia does not own and cannot license. Every Chinese instrument (curfew, spending cap, content edit) depends on the publisher being reachable by the regulator; in Indonesia most publishers are foreign entities with no local establishment. This is structural and will not change.

2. NO MASS REAL-NAME IDENTITY BINDING, AND CULTURAL RESISTANCE TO IT. China's minor restrictions are technically enforceable only because every account maps to a verified national ID and platforms run facial recognition. Indonesia's prepaid, cash-and-pulsa digital economy is built on the opposite premise, and post-2021 Dukcapil/BPJS data-leak scandals have made mandatory ID binding politically toxic. Without this, playtime curfews would be unenforceable theatre.

3. THE STATE HAS THE OPPOSITE ECONOMIC INTEREST. China could crush its domestic industry in 2021 because Chinese firms owned the industry — the value destroyed was recaptured domestically and offset by exports. Indonesia captures 0.5-5% of its own market's value; restricting play destroys tax revenue and consumer surplus while the profits it might discipline sit offshore. The state has little leverage and little to gain, so it will regulate content and age gates rather than time and spend.

4. NO GAOKAO-EQUIVALENT SOCIAL PRESSURE. China's minor gaming restrictions were coupled to the double-reduction education campaign and a national obsession with a single high-stakes exam. Indonesia abolished the UN national exam in 2021 and has a far less zero-sum academic-competition culture, removing the strongest political motive for restricting children's leisure time.

5. DEMOGRAPHIC AND FISCAL ASYMMETRY. China's crackdown was legible as demographic policy (a one-child generation's health and fertility). Indonesia has a demographic dividend and frames youth digital engagement as an asset, not a scarcity to be protected.

6. ARCHIPELAGIC AND INCOME STRUCTURE CAPS THE MONETIZATION MODEL, NOT JUST THE REGULATION. China's whale-driven gacha economy assumes high disposable income concentrated in dense cities. Indonesia's low ARPU, prepaid data, and dispersed geography mean the Indonesian market will skew permanently toward ad-monetized, low-data, low-spec titles. So the specific Chinese harm pattern (children spending five- and six-figure sums on gacha, triggering parental outrage and then regulation) will manifest in a muted, distributed form — which paradoxically reduces the political trigger for restriction while the aggregate harm (time, attention, gambling adjacency) still accumulates.

7. THE HARM VECTOR HAS ALREADY BEEN CAPTURED BY A DIFFERENT POLICY FRAME. In Indonesia, the dominant child-digital-harm narrative is judi online and pornography, not gaming per se. Gaming regulation is being pulled along as a rider on gambling and child-safety enforcement, which means Indonesia will likely end up with gambling-adjacency rules and age ratings rather than China's playtime architecture — a different regulatory species entirely.

8. OWNERSHIP DRIFT AWAY FROM CHINA. The March 2026 agreement to sell Moonton to Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group removes Indonesia's single most important game from Chinese ownership. Gulf sovereign capital is now a competing transmission channel with different regulatory sensitivities, further weakening the 'China → Indonesia' pipe for governance norms even as content flows continue.
tahun_masuk_indonesia: Already arrived, in stages. Consumption: 2016 (MLBB launch; Free Fire 2017) — no lag. Esports institutionalization: 2018-2020 (Asian Games 2018 demonstration event in Jakarta/Palembang; PBESI formation; MPL franchising). Protective regulation, first binding step: 2025-2026 — PP 17/2025 signed 28 March 2025 and effective 1 April 2025, with platform obligations phased from 28 March 2026, plus IGRS relaunched 11 October 2025 and mandatory from 2026. Chinese-style hard playtime/spending restriction: not yet arrived; earliest plausible legislative appearance 2028-2030 [uncertain]. Mini-game wave (China's 2023-2025 growth engine): first meaningful Indonesian presence 2026-2027.
tahun_mainstream_indonesia: Consumption is already mainstream (2019-2021; roughly 155-190m players, gaming is the default youth leisure activity nationwide). Esports is mainstream (2021-2023; MPL viewership in the tens of millions, state recognition, brand sponsorship from banks and telcos). PROTECTIVE REGULATION becomes mainstream — meaning actually enforced and behaviour-changing rather than paper compliance — around 2027-2029: I expect 2026-2027 to be a compliance-theatre period (age labels appear, little behavioural change), with real enforcement arriving only after a high-profile incident forces it. Mini-games mainstream 2028-2029. Domestic development reaching a meaningful share (10%+) of domestic spending: not before 2032-2035, if ever [uncertain].
tahun_puncak_indonesia: Consumption/player-count peak: roughly 2028-2032, when internet penetration approaches saturation (~90%) and the Gen Alpha cohort fully enters gaming age; after that growth converts to ARPU rather than users, mirroring China's post-2021 pattern. Revenue peak: later, ~2032-2035, as income growth lifts ARPU from a low base (Indonesia's per-capita income today is roughly where China's was in 2013-2015). Esports peak: 2026-2029 for audience and hype — Indonesia's esports audience is already broad, franchise economics are already strained by weak sponsorship depth, and China's plateau (audience flat since 2021 with 80% of income from livestreaming) is the template; expect Indonesian consolidation and team failures from ~2028. Regulatory-intensity peak: 2029-2032 — the moment when accumulated harm data, an election cycle, and a trigger incident coincide. Peak geography: Greater Jakarta, Bandung and Surabaya for industry and esports infrastructure; consumption peak intensity is actually in second- and third-tier cities and outside Java, where gaming has fewer leisure substitutes. [uncertain — all peak-year estimates are analytical projections]
skenario_percepatan: Accelerators for REGULATION: (1) a nationally reported tragedy involving a child and gaming/gacha spending or online gambling — Indonesia's regulatory clock historically starts with a viral case; (2) formal legal classification of gacha/loot boxes as gambling under judi online enforcement, which would instantly drag major titles into an existing enforcement machine; (3) Australia's under-16 social media ban proving operable, giving Indonesian regulators a copyable technical template; (4) a Kemenkes national prevalence study quantifying gaming disorder; (5) integration of INA Digital/IKD with app-store age signals, which removes the enforceability excuse; (6) an election cycle where child digital safety becomes a campaign plank. Accelerators for the INDUSTRY/mini-game wave: TikTok Indonesia launching in-app game monetization; a Chinese mini-game publisher establishing an Indonesian entity; Perpres 19/2024 implementing regulations actually releasing fiscal incentives; Gulf capital (post-Moonton) investing in Southeast Asian studios; and cheap AI-assisted content pipelines lowering the cost of shipping a game below the Indonesian studio capital threshold.
dampak_lapangan_kerja:
JOBS CREATED (already visible in Indonesia, expanding):
- Esports ecosystem roles: professional players, coaches, analysts, team managers, tournament operations/production crew, casters/shoutcasters, observers, referees, esports venue staff. Note the pyramid is brutally narrow — Indonesia has roughly a few hundred salaried tier-1 players against hundreds of thousands of aspirants.
- Content and community: gaming streamers and YouTubers, clip editors, thumbnail designers, community/Discord managers, talent managers and MCN-equivalent agencies, esports journalists.
- Commercial services around foreign titles: localization and Indonesian voice-over, customer support/CS outsourcing, community moderation, user-acquisition and performance marketing agencies, influencer marketing, top-up merchants and payment agents (UniPin/Codashop reseller networks reach into kiosks and warung).
- Compliance and safety, a genuinely new category from 2026: IGRS compliance officers, age-assurance/verification engineers, trust-and-safety analysts, content moderators, child online-safety specialists at platforms and at Komdigi.
- Clinical and educational: behavioural-addiction psychologists and psychiatrists (already capacity-constrained — RSJ Menur has exceeded inpatient capacity), school counsellors specializing in digital wellbeing, parent-education trainers.
- Development-side (small but the highest-value): Unity/Unreal engineers, technical artists, 3D and character artists, animators, level designers, game economy designers, LiveOps managers, QA, build engineers, backend/netcode engineers. Art and animation outsourcing for foreign publishers is the most realistic mass-employment path (the Vietnam/Philippines model).

JOBS CHANGED:
- Warnet/internet cafe operators shifting from browsing to gaming cafes and esports venues, and now to console/VR corners.
- Traditional sports coaching and youth-development organizations absorbing esports as a discipline.
- Advertising and media planning, as gaming and streaming take share from TV.
- Telco product managers building gaming-specific data products.

JOBS LOST OR DEVALUED:
- Physical game/DVD retail and console rental (already gone).
- Traditional warnet browsing businesses.
- Generic media/broadcast production roles displaced by streaming-native production.
- Boosting/account-trading grey work, which regulation will criminalize or squeeze.
- In China specifically, the 2021-2022 crackdown eliminated roughly 14,000 gaming-related firms (some counts up to 140,000 including adjacent services) and triggered layoffs at Tencent, NetEase and 37Games — the direct lesson is that this employment is highly regulation-elastic and can vanish in a single policy cycle.

NET ASSESSMENT FOR INDONESIA: as long as Indonesia captures under 5% of its own market's value, gaming creates mostly LOW-VALUE, DOWNSTREAM jobs (top-up agents, streamers, community managers, tournament crew) rather than HIGH-VALUE upstream engineering jobs. The employment story is therefore currently a consumption-servicing story, not an industrial one — the opposite of China, where the sector employs hundreds of thousands in development and exports USD 20bn+.
dampak_kelas_menengah:
(1) HOUSEHOLD BUDGET LEAKAGE. Gaming top-ups are a small but persistent drain on aspirational middle-class and lower-middle-class households, and unlike China's whale economy the Indonesian pattern is many small, hard-to-notice pulsa-based transactions — which makes it harder for parents to detect and easier to normalize. Because most spending flows to foreign publishers, this is a direct consumption leakage out of the domestic economy at a time when Indonesia's middle class is already contracting (the widely reported shrinkage of the aspiring middle class since 2019).

(2) PARENTING BURDEN AND MENTAL-HEALTH COSTS. The middle class bears the visible cost first because it is the segment that seeks treatment: the 28% y/y rise in child psychiatric visits for gadget addiction, and the 1,856 cases at RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan, are disproportionately urban middle-class families with the awareness and means to present at a hospital. Private behavioural-therapy costs are not covered adequately by BPJS, creating a new out-of-pocket burden.

(3) STATUS AND ASPIRATION DISTORTION. Esports offers a visible, aspirational mobility path — 'become a pro player' — that is statistically far worse than the educational paths it competes with. This mirrors China's experience where esports vocational programmes drew students who then found few paid roles. For middle-class families, the risk is a mis-allocated education decision made at 15-17.

(4) NEW MIDDLE-CLASS OCCUPATIONS. Conversely, the sector genuinely creates middle-class-compatible careers: game developers, technical artists, community and marketing managers, tournament producers, and compliance officers. Salaries in Indonesian game development are modest but competitive with general IT, and outsourcing work pays in foreign currency.

(5) GAMBLING ADJACENCY IS THE SHARPEST MIDDLE-CLASS RISK. The judi online crisis has demonstrated that the same demographic and the same payment rails move fluidly between gaming top-ups and gambling deposits. For lower-middle-class households, a gacha habit and a slot-app habit are separated by one advertisement.

(6) TIME-USE. Gaming is the cheapest per-hour entertainment available (a Rp 50,000 data package can fill a month), which makes it structurally attractive precisely to households under economic pressure — a demand pattern that will intensify, not weaken, if Indonesian consumer downgrading continues.
dampak_daerah_non_jawa:
HIGHLY RELEVANT OUTSIDE JAVA — arguably more so than in Jakarta, and this is under-appreciated in Indonesian policy discourse.

CONSUMPTION IS NATIONAL, NOT JAVA-CENTRIC. Internet penetration is 76.96% in rural areas versus 83.56% urban (APJII 2025) — a gap of under seven points. Mobile games require little bandwidth (Free Fire is deliberately low-spec and low-data, which is why it dominates in lower-income and non-Java regions), so the consumption trend has already fully diffused. The documented extreme case of a 17-year-old consuming 30GB/month purely on Free Fire came from Bangka Belitung, not Jakarta, and RSJ Sungailiat there recorded 68 new addiction cases in two months (+35%). RSJ Lampung and RSJ Menur (Surabaya) report the same trajectory. The harm is distributed nationally while treatment capacity (54 psychiatric hospitals, heavily Java-weighted) is not.

WHY NON-JAVA EXPOSURE IS HIGHER, NOT LOWER: fewer alternative leisure and extracurricular options, fewer formal youth employment opportunities, weaker school counselling capacity, lower parental digital literacy, and higher rates of children left with smartphones while parents work. Gaming's substitution value is greatest where the substitutes are scarcest.

INDUSTRY AND ESPORTS ARE JAVA-CENTRIC. Development studios cluster in Bandung, Jakarta, Yogyakarta and Surabaya; MPL and franchise teams, esports venues, production facilities, publisher offices, and game-related university programmes are almost entirely on Java (with Bali as a small outlier). Esports talent from outside Java must migrate to Jakarta/Bandung to turn pro, creating a familiar centre-periphery extraction pattern: the regions supply players and spending, Java captures the salaries and margins.

POLICY IMPLICATION: any protective regulation designed and enforced from Jakarta will bite least where harm is greatest. Conversely, the most scalable non-Java opportunity is not esports venues but remote-capable digital work — art outsourcing, QA, localization, community moderation — which can be located anywhere with decent connectivity, and which regional polytechnics could realistically supply.
jurusan_terancam:
This trend threatens fewer majors by direct substitution than by ATTENTION AND RELEVANCE EROSION, plus one important category of over-supplied new majors:

1. ESPORTS-MANAGEMENT AND 'PRO PLAYER' PROGRAMMES THEMSELVES — the single most important warning. China opened 'Esports and Management' as a vocational major in 2016-2017; roughly 30 colleges by 2019 and many more later, but placement outcomes disappointed and the pipeline produced far more graduates than the industry's paid roles, with graduates diverted into journalism, casting and event operations. Indonesian institutions are now rushing into the same space (UI Vokasi added esports to its curriculum; multiple private campuses market 'jurusan esports'). Programmes built around competitive play rather than transferable business/production/technical skills will become the clearest example of an over-supplied major.

2. TRADITIONAL BROADCAST AND TELEVISION PRODUCTION (Ilmu Komunikasi - Broadcasting, Penyiaran) — audiences and ad budgets have migrated to streaming and gaming content; linear-TV-specific curricula are the most exposed.

3. CONVENTIONAL PRINT/SPORTS JOURNALISM — displaced by creator-led coverage.

4. GENERIC DESAIN KOMUNIKASI VISUAL / 2D graphic design without real-time 3D, technical art, or engine skills — the entry-level static-design market is being compressed simultaneously by generative AI and by demand shifting toward interactive/real-time assets.

5. CONVENTIONAL ILMU KEOLAHRAGAAN / PENJASKES that treats sport purely physically — as esports enters the national sport system, these programmes must absorb it or lose relevance in the youth-sport administration job market.

6. GENERAL 'TEKNIK INFORMATIKA' WITHOUT SPECIALIZATION — not threatened by gaming specifically, but the gaming path illustrates the broader point that undifferentiated IT graduates lose to specialists.

7. TOURISM/HOSPITALITY AND CONVENTIONAL ENTERTAINMENT MANAGEMENT programmes assuming physical-venue leisure demand from youth.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT: 'threatened' here means reduced relevance and worse placement, not disappearance. The honest framing for Indonesian universities is that the threat is to programmes whose graduates cannot do anything a game studio, platform, or regulator will pay for.
jurusan_dibutuhkan:
TECHNICAL / DEVELOPMENT (highest value, scarcest in Indonesia):
- Game programming: C++ and C#, Unity and Unreal Engine, gameplay systems, physics, rendering fundamentals.
- Technical art and real-time 3D: shaders, rigging, optimization for low-spec Android devices (the specific skill Indonesia's own market requires and that Chinese publishers hire for).
- Backend and netcode: distributed systems, matchmaking, anti-cheat, live service architecture, cloud cost engineering.
- Game economy design and monetization analytics — the discipline that actually determines profitability; combines behavioural economics, statistics and product management. Almost absent from Indonesian curricula.
- LiveOps and product management for games: cohort analysis, retention/LTV modelling, A/B testing, seasonal content planning.
- Data science applied to player behaviour, churn and fraud detection.
- AI/ML applied to games: procedural content, NPC behaviour, AI-assisted art pipelines, plus the emerging role of AI content-safety tooling.
- Audio design and adaptive music; motion capture and animation.
- QA automation and build/release engineering — the most accessible entry point and the natural base for outsourcing employment.

CREATIVE / NARRATIVE:
- Game design and systems design (distinct from art), level design, narrative design and worldbuilding; adaptation of Indonesian mythology and history into globally legible IP (the Lokapala/Nusantara path).
- Localization and transcreation (Indonesian ↔ Mandarin, English, Japanese) — a direct, immediate earner given Chinese publishers' Indonesian expansion.

BUSINESS / OPERATIONS:
- Esports business management: sponsorship sales, league operations, athlete contracts and welfare, broadcast production management, venue operations.
- Creator/talent management and digital media rights.
- User acquisition and performance marketing for apps.

GOVERNANCE / SAFETY — the fastest-growing new category from 2026:
- Trust and safety, content moderation policy, age assurance and identity engineering.
- Digital child-protection law and platform compliance (IGRS, PP Tunas, DSA-style regimes) — lawyers and compliance officers who understand both code and regulation.
- Clinical and counselling psychology specializing in behavioural addiction (gaming disorder, gambling), plus digital-wellbeing curriculum design for schools. Indonesia's psychiatric system is already over capacity on exactly this caseload.
- Data protection and privacy engineering (PDP Law compliance for children's data).

CROSS-CUTTING: for Indonesian students, the highest expected-value combination is a genuine engineering or art-production skill PLUS English/Mandarin PLUS portfolio evidence — because the realistic first employer is a foreign publisher or an outsourcing client, not a domestic studio.
china_education_response:
China's education system responded to gaming and esports faster and more institutionally than any other country, then partially corrected:

1. VOCATIONAL MAJOR CREATION (2016-2017). In September 2016 the Department of Vocational and Adult Education of the Ministry of Education added 'Esports and Management' (电子竞技运动与管理) to the supplementary catalogue of higher vocational majors, for implementation from 2017. This is the single clearest instance of a state adding a major specifically in response to a digital-economy trend. Hunan Sports Vocational College ran an esports class of 40 students in autumn 2017; roughly 30 colleges offered esports-related programmes by 2019, and the number grew into the hundreds across vocational institutions in subsequent years.

2. UNIVERSITY-LEVEL PROGRAMMES (2017 onward). The Communication University of China opened a digital media art programme with an esports analysis direction (small cohorts, ~20 students) in 2017; Sichuan Film and Television University, Shanghai institutions and others followed. Curricula covered event operations, commentary, data analysis, team management and broadcast production — deliberately NOT 'how to play'.

3. OCCUPATIONAL RECOGNITION (2019). MOHRSS formally recognized 'esports operator' (电子竞技运营师) and 'esports player' (电子竞技员) as official new occupations in April 2019, creating a formal skills-standard and certification pathway — the step Indonesia has not taken.

4. GAME DEVELOPMENT EDUCATION. Game programming and art were absorbed into existing digital media technology, digital media art, animation, and software engineering programmes rather than being made a standalone major, supported by a very large CS graduate base (China produces well over a million CS/engineering graduates annually). Industry-academia arrangements with Tencent, NetEase and Perfect World (Perfect World Education runs its own training institutes) supplied vocational-to-industry pipelines.

5. THE CORRECTION (2019-2022). Placement outcomes for esports graduates disappointed: the industry's 'talent gap' rhetoric referred mostly to operations and content roles, while students enrolled expecting to become players. After the 2021 crackdown and the 2021-2022 licence freeze and layoffs, enrolment enthusiasm cooled, some programmes were quietly renamed or folded into broader digital-media majors, and messaging shifted toward 'esports industry management' rather than competitive play. The lesson China learned and Indonesia has not yet absorbed: create programmes for the industry's actual job pyramid, not for its visible apex.

6. THE RESTRICTIVE SIDE OF THE EDUCATION RESPONSE. The gaming curbs were designed to sit alongside the 'double reduction' policy (July 2021) limiting private tutoring and homework, and alongside the revised Law on the Protection of Minors (effective 1 June 2021) which added an Internet Protection chapter obliging schools, families and platforms to prevent minors' internet addiction. Schools were tasked with digital-literacy and anti-addiction education, and the State Council's Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Cyberspace (effective 1 January 2024) made 'minor mode' obligations explicit across devices, app stores and applications. Education policy and platform policy were deliberately coordinated — a coherence Indonesia's fragmented ministries currently lack.
respons_kebijakan_china:
CHINA'S POLICY TOOLKIT, IN THE ORDER IT WAS DEPLOYED, WITH ADOPTABILITY ASSESSMENT FOR INDONESIA:

1. GACHA/LOOT-BOX PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE (Ministry of Culture interim measures, effective 1 May 2017). Publishers must disclose the drop rates of random-draw items. World-first, low-cost, high-transparency, and it does not restrict anyone's freedom to play. HIGHLY ADOPTABLE by Indonesia — could be attached to IGRS technical standards immediately and enforced through app-store listing requirements. This is the single best preemptive policy Indonesia could copy.

2. REAL-NAME REGISTRATION (from 2007, hardened 2019-2021) plus platform-side facial recognition ('Midnight Patrol', Tencent 2021). Enables everything downstream. PARTIALLY ADOPTABLE — Indonesia should require age assurance (not necessarily full ID binding), using device/OS-level age signals from Google and Apple, which is far cheaper and privacy-safer than a national game ID.

3. AGE-TIERED IN-GAME SPENDING CAPS (2019 notice: monthly caps scaled by age band). ADOPTABLE and arguably more urgent for Indonesia than time limits, because the financial-harm channel (and its bleed into judi online) is Indonesia's sharpest documented risk. Should be paired with a mandatory refund mechanism for verified minor purchases.

4. PLAYTIME CURFEWS FOR MINORS (2019: 90 min/weekday, 3h/holiday, 22:00-08:00 blackout; 2021: 1 hour on Fri/Sat/Sun/holidays only). Effective on paper — CADPA/Gamma reported >75% of minor gamers playing under three hours a week by late 2022 — but only because of the real-name substrate. LOW ADOPTABILITY for Indonesia without identity infrastructure; would produce circumvention and disrespect for the law. Note also the cautionary precedent: South Korea repealed its own shutdown law in 2021 after a decade of poor results.

5. LICENSING CHOKEPOINT (banhao) AND APPROVAL FREEZES (2018; July 2021-April 2022). The most powerful instrument, and the most economically destructive — roughly 14,000 firms closed (up to 140,000 by broader definitions), Tencent lost close to USD 200bn of market value in 2018 and ~USD 60bn in one day in August 2021. NOT ADOPTABLE and should not be copied: Indonesia lacks the sovereign distribution layer, and would destroy its nascent local studios while foreign titles route around it.

6. BAN ON ADDICTIVE MONETIZATION MECHANICS (December 2023 draft: monthly spend caps ~RMB 400, ban on daily-login and consecutive-recharge rewards, ban on item auctions). Wiped ~USD 80bn off Tencent and NetEase and was WITHDRAWN in January 2024. The lesson for Indonesia is about process, not substance: regulate monetization through disclosure and defaults, consult industry before publishing, and never surprise a listed market — otherwise the policy dies and nothing is protected.

7. LEGAL CODIFICATION (revised Law on the Protection of Minors, effective 1 June 2021, adding an Internet Protection chapter; State Council Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Cyberspace, effective 1 January 2024; mandatory 'minor mode' across devices, app stores and apps). ADOPTABLE — Indonesia's PP 17/2025 is the structural equivalent but currently thinner. The specific Chinese innovation worth copying is placing obligations at the DEVICE and APP-STORE layer, not only on individual apps, because that is where enforcement is tractable against foreign publishers.

8. CONTENT REVIEW AND CULTURAL REQUIREMENTS. Politically specific to China; NOT ADOPTABLE and not desirable.

9. INDUSTRY SELF-REGULATION WITH STATE BACKING (CADPA/GPC publishing compliance progress reports, an industry age-rating standard). ADOPTABLE and cheap: Indonesia should require a publisher self-declaration regime under IGRS with audit and penalty, rather than trying to review hundreds of thousands of titles centrally.

10. SEPARATION OF ESPORTS FROM 'GAMING HARM'. China simultaneously restricted minors and promoted esports as a legitimate sport and industry (Asian Games medal event 2023, city-level subsidies). ADOPTABLE, and in fact Indonesia is already doing this via Kemenpora recognition and Perpres 19/2024 — but China coupled promotion with restriction, whereas Indonesia has so far only done promotion.

SYNTHESIS OF THE PREEMPTIVE PACKAGE INDONESIA COULD ADOPT NOW: probability disclosure + minor spending caps with refund rights + device/app-store-level age assurance + IGRS enforcement with real penalties + gambling-adjacency rules. That package captures most of China's protective benefit while avoiding the instruments (banhao, curfews, facial recognition) that Indonesia cannot enforce and should not want.
rekomendasi_kebijakan_indonesia:
1. MANDATE GACHA/LOOT-BOX PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE via a Permen Komdigi attached to IGRS technical standards, following China's 2017 precedent. Cheapest, fastest, least contested protective measure available.
2. LEGISLATE MINOR SPENDING CAPS AND A STATUTORY REFUND RIGHT for unauthorized minor in-game purchases, enforced at the payment layer (QRIS, e-wallets, telco pulsa billing) rather than only at the publisher — because the payment rails are domestic and reachable, while publishers are not.
3. CLOSE THE GAMBLING-ADJACENCY GAP explicitly. Define in regulation the line between gacha, item trading/marketplaces, and gambling; ban cash-out and third-party item resale markets for titles rated below 18+; require publishers to block gambling advertising in-game. This is the highest-priority item given ~200,000 children already exposed to judi online.
4. PUT OBLIGATIONS AT THE DEVICE AND APP-STORE LAYER. Require Google Play and the App Store to transmit a verified age band to apps distributed in Indonesia, and to enforce IGRS ratings at download. risiko_sosial_indonesia:
1. GAMING AS THE ON-RAMP TO ONLINE GAMBLING — the highest-priority Indonesian risk and the one with no Chinese analogue at this scale. China eliminated consumer online gambling early; Indonesia did not, so Indonesian children move between gacha, item trading, and slot apps through the same payment rails, the same advertising surfaces, and the same social groups. Komdigi reported in 2026 that nearly 200,000 Indonesian children have been exposed to online gambling, and psychiatric hospitals began handling child gambling-addiction cases in 2025. Without a clear regulatory line between gacha and gambling, gaming will keep functioning as a recruitment funnel.
2. A MENTAL-HEALTH CAPACITY CRISIS ALREADY IN PROGRESS. Child and adolescent psychiatric visits for gadget addiction rose 28% y/y in late 2025; RSJ Soeharto Heerdjan logged 1,856 cases (62% game addiction); RSJ Menur has exceeded inpatient capacity and is queueing patients; RSJ Sungailiat in Bangka Belitung logged 68 new cases in two months (+35%); RSJ Lampung reports the same. Indonesia has roughly 54 psychiatric hospitals handling all addiction types for a population of 284m, concentrated on Java. Demand is outrunning supply now, before any of the growth this trend still has ahead of it.
3. FINANCIAL EXTRACTION FROM POOR HOUSEHOLDS WITH NO REFUND RIGHT. Pulsa- and voucher-based top-up requires no ID, no bank account and no parental visibility; a child can spend a household's weekly food budget in an afternoon with no practical recourse against a foreign publisher. Indonesia has no statutory minor-refund mechanism and no spending caps.
4. UNENFORCEABLE REGULATION BREEDING GENERAL NON-COMPLIANCE. If Indonesia adopts age gates it cannot verify, the predictable result is universal false age declaration, normalized VPN use, and a population of minors and parents who have learned that digital law is optional — which will poison enforcement of the PDP Law and future child-safety rules too.
5. EDUCATIONAL MISALLOCATION AT SCALE. A generation channelled toward an esports career pyramid that cannot support it, encouraged by universities marketing 'jurusan esports' — China ran this experiment from 2016 and the graduate outcomes were poor.
6. EXPLOITATION OF MINOR ESPORTS ATHLETES. No standard contracts, no minimum age, no education-continuity requirement, no salary escrow, no mental-health provision. Teenagers are already signing multi-year agreements with Indonesian organizations.
7. CONTINUED VALUE LEAKAGE. With 95-99.5% of domestic game spending flowing to foreign publishers, Indonesia absorbs the full social cost of a mature industry while capturing almost none of the tax base or employment that would fund mitigation — the defining asymmetry of this trend for Indonesia.
8. NON-JAVA HARM CONCENTRATION WITH JAVA-CONCENTRATED TREATMENT. Rural internet penetration (76.96%) is close to urban (83.56%) and leisure substitutes are scarcer outside Java, so exposure is highest exactly where clinical, counselling and school-support capacity is thinnest.
9. DATA AND PRIVACY RISK FROM THE REMEDY. Any serious age-assurance regime will collect children's identity data. Given Indonesia's record of large-scale government and platform data breaches, a poorly designed minor-verification system could itself become the harm — an argument for device-level age signals over centralized ID databases.
10. DISPLACEMENT RATHER THAN REDUCTION. China's experience shows that restricting games without addressing the attention economy simply moves minors to short video. Indonesia, where TikTok penetration is among the world's highest, would see this substitution immediately and more strongly.
unintended_consequences:
IN CHINA (observed):
- Time freed by the gaming ban went to short video rather than study; reporting after the 2021 rules found teenagers were not studying more. The state solved a measurable problem by displacing it into a less-measured one, and later had to regulate minor mode across all apps (2024) as a result.
- Enforcement created a grey market in identity: rented and purchased adult accounts, grandparents' IDs, and eventually facial recognition applied to children — normalizing biometric surveillance of minors as a child-protection measure.
- The licence freeze intended to discipline giants instead killed roughly 14,000 small firms and entrenched the Tencent/NetEase duopoly, reducing content diversity.
- Restriction accelerated globalization: shut out of domestic growth, Chinese publishers pushed overseas, reaching USD 20.45bn in export revenue by 2025 — meaning China's domestic child-protection policy directly intensified the commercial pressure on markets like Indonesia. Indonesia is, in a real sense, absorbing the displaced output of China's own crackdown.
- The December 2023 monetization draft's withdrawal after an USD 80bn market rout demonstrated regulatory capture-by-market-reaction, leaving the coercive mechanics (login streaks, recharge inducements) legal to this day.
- Esports education created expectations the industry could not meet, producing a cohort of disappointed graduates — a policy-induced labour mismatch.
- Anti-addiction rules pushed some minors toward unapproved foreign titles via VPN accelerators, prompting further enforcement (Tencent cutting off booster access to unapproved games in 2022) — an enforcement spiral.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA:
- IGRS enforcement will initially produce labelling compliance without behavioural change, while inadvertently pushing users toward unrated third-party APK distribution — increasing malware and scam exposure, a harm larger than the one being solved.
- Any age gate without verification will train an entire generation to lie about their age, degrading the reliability of all age-based digital policy including gambling and pornography controls.
- Restricting games while leaving short video untouched will shift minors' time to TikTok, where Indonesia's exposure is even greater than China's was.
- Promoting esports (Perpres 19/2024, Kemenpora recognition) while simultaneously warning about game addiction will produce mixed public messaging that undermines both objectives.
- Payment-layer restrictions on top-ups may push transactions to informal reseller networks and crypto, reducing traceability precisely for the judi online cases enforcement is trying to catch.
- A crackdown framed around 'Chinese games' could arrive as economic nationalism rather than child protection, harming Indonesian studios who depend on the same platforms and publishers while doing nothing for children.
- Positive unintended consequence: compliance obligations from PP Tunas and IGRS may create the first genuinely well-paid, non-engineering digital careers in Indonesia (trust and safety, compliance, age assurance) and give local studios a home-field regulatory advantage over foreign publishers who find compliance costly.

kasus_china:
CASE 1 — TENCENT / HONOR OF KINGS AS THE POLICY LIGHTNING ROD. Honor of Kings (launched November 2015) became China's defining mobile game and the named target of the 3 August 2021 Economic Information Daily 'spiritual opium' (精神鸦片) article, which cited a student playing eight hours a day. Tencent lost roughly USD 60bn in market value in a single session; within days it announced deeper self-imposed restrictions for under-18s (90 minutes on ordinary days, 3 hours on holidays) ahead of the regulator. Tencent then deployed 'Midnight Patrol' facial recognition to catch minors using adult accounts. By the mid-2020s minors accounted for well under 1% of Tencent's domestic games gross receipts [uncertain on exact figure]. This is the clearest demonstration that in China, anticipatory self-regulation by the dominant firm was faster and more effective than the formal rule that followed.

CASE 2 — THE 30 AUGUST 2021 NPPA NOTICE AND ITS MEASURED EFFECT. Under-18s restricted to one hour, 20:00-21:00, on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays only — 3 hours per week, down from the 13.5 hours permitted under the November 2019 rules, a 78% reduction by decree. By November 2022 CADPA's Game Publishing Committee and Gamma Data reported that over 75% of minor gamers played under three hours per week and declared the addiction problem 'basically resolved'. The counter-case: contemporaneous reporting found that teenagers were not studying more; the time went to short video.

CASE 3 — THE LICENCE FREEZE AND THE 14,000 CLOSURES. Approvals were frozen from July 2021 to April 2022 (after an earlier nine-month freeze in 2018). Roughly 14,000 gaming studios and gaming-related firms shut down (up to 140,000 by broader definitions), with layoffs and cancellations at Tencent, NetEase and 37Games. The regulatory instrument aimed at protecting children destroyed the small-studio layer of the industry.

CASE 4 — THE DECEMBER 2023 DRAFT THAT WAS WITHDRAWN. On 22 December 2023 the NPPA published draft 'Measures for the Administration of Online Games' — 8 chapters, 64 articles, roughly 10 of them new — proposing monthly in-game spending caps (~RMB 400), a ban on daily-login, first-recharge and consecutive-recharge rewards, and a ban on item auctions. Tencent and NetEase shed roughly USD 80bn combined. The consultation closed 22 January 2024 and the draft was quietly removed from the NPPA website; it was never enacted. The single most instructive case for Indonesia: the state blinked when the economic cost became visible, and the coercive monetization mechanics remain legal.

CASE 5 — GACHA PROBABILITY DISCLOSURE, EFFECTIVE 1 MAY 2017. Ministry of Culture interim measures required publishers to disclose random-draw probabilities — years before Western regulators seriously debated loot boxes. Cheap, non-restrictive, and still the best-value protective policy China invented.

CASE 6 — ESPORTS BUILT AND THEN PLATEAUED. MOE added 'Esports and Management' to the vocational catalogue in September 2016; MOHRSS recognized esports player and esports operator as official occupations in April 2019; Hangzhou hosted esports as a full Asian Games medal event in 2023. Yet the audience has moved from 489.2m (2021) to 495.3m (2025) — 6m in four years — while 80.81% of the RMB 29.33bn industry income comes from livestreaming. A fully institutionalized, fully plateaued sector, and the template for where Indonesian esports economics are heading.

CASE 7 — THE 2025 NUMBERS AS THE MATURE-STATE PICTURE. Domestic market RMB 350.789bn (+7.68%), 683m users (+1.35%), mini-games RMB 53.535bn (+34.39%) generating over half of all incremental growth, overseas revenue USD 20.45bn. Growth now comes from new formats and foreign markets, not new domestic players — the export pressure that lands directly on Indonesia.

catatan_kontradiksi_data:
1. INDONESIAN MARKET SIZE VARIES BY 4x. USD 4.28bn (2025, Xsolla/industry estimates) vs ~USD 2.0-2.5bn / Rp 41.3tn (Kemenperin-linked industry studies) vs USD 1.117bn (Statista 2023, cited in Perpres 19/2024 commentary) vs a projection of USD 6.66bn by 2034 (which would be inconsistent with a USD 4.28bn 2025 base at 8% CAGR). The divergence reflects whether hardware, ad revenue, esports and grey-market top-ups are included. Treat USD 2.5-4.3bn as the plausible band; do not cite a single point estimate.
2. INDONESIAN ESPORTS MARKET ESTIMATES ARE UNUSABLE. Published figures range from USD 1.8bn (2025, 24.1% CAGR) to USD 11.75-18.54m — a difference of two orders of magnitude, indicating that some vendors measure ecosystem spending and others measure only tournament/league income. Flagged as uncertain and excluded from analytical conclusions.
3. LOCAL DEVELOPER SHARE: 0.4% (Kemenperin, cited 2021) vs 0.5% (October 2025 study) vs 5% (February 2026 report). These are not reconcilable as a time series — they likely use different denominators (all consumer spending vs. domestically-published titles vs. registered-studio revenue). The safe statement is 'under 5%, and possibly under 1%'.
4. INDONESIAN PLAYER COUNT: 155m (on a 274m population base, an older figure) vs ~190-192m projected for 2025. 'Gamer' definitions include anyone who plays any mobile game, which inflates counts relative to China's 683m on a 1.41bn population.
5. CHINA FIRM CLOSURES: 14,000 vs 140,000 during the 2021-2022 freeze. This is a definitional split (game studios and publishers vs. all gaming-related firms including advertising and merchandising), not a factual dispute, but the 140,000 figure is frequently quoted without that qualification.
6. CHINA MARKET REVENUE FRAMING: RMB 350.789bn (2025) is 'actual sales revenue of the domestic games market' per CADPA/Gamma; some English-language sources render this as roughly USD 48-50bn while others use different exchange-rate assumptions or add export revenue, producing inconsistent 'China games market' totals.
7. EFFECTIVENESS OF CHINA'S MINOR RESTRICTIONS IS CONTESTED. CADPA/Gamma (Nov 2022) reported >75% of minor gamers under three hours weekly and declared the problem 'basically resolved' — but the reporting body is the industry association, giving it an interest in demonstrating compliance. Independent reporting found time displaced to short video rather than study, and documented widespread use of adult IDs. Both can be true: the rule worked on the metric it measured and failed on the outcome it was meant to serve.
8. IGRS 'FIRST IN SOUTHEAST ASIA' FRAMING IS MISLEADING. Some 2025 coverage described the October 2025 IGRS as the first national game classification system in Southeast Asia; IGRS itself dates to 2016 (Permenkominfo 11/2016). The accurate statement is that 2025-2026 marks the first serious ENFORCEMENT of a system that has existed on paper for nine years.
9. PP TUNAS TIMELINE: sources variously give 28 March 2025 (signing), 1 April 2025 (entry into force), and 28 March 2026 (phased platform obligations / end of transition). All three dates appear in reporting and are not contradictory, but are often conflated.
10. MOONTON OWNERSHIP IS IN TRANSITION AS OF THIS RESEARCH DATE. The Savvy Games Group acquisition was agreed 20 March 2026 at >USD 6bn but requires regulatory approval expected in Q2-Q3 2026. Any statement that MLBB is 'Chinese-owned' or 'Saudi-owned' is timing-sensitive; as of August 2026 the closing status is not confirmed in available sources.
11. INDONESIAN HOSPITAL ADDICTION DATA comes from regional media reporting individual facilities rather than a consolidated national Kemenkes dataset; the 28% y/y figure covers a two-month window (Oct-Nov 2025), which is a narrow base for a trend claim.
